source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for prefill. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: single-node 8xA30 24GB, PCIe Gen4 (no NVLink), vLLM-class continuous-batching server, decoder-only dense model, FP16/BF16 weights, fixed model and fixed sampling params.

Goal: falsifiable test that prefill is compute-bound (GEMM-dominated) while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.

Mechanism: prefill runs all P prompt tokens through attention/MLP in one parallel pass, so per-layer work is a (P x d) x (d x d) GEMM whose arithmetic intensity grows with P; weights are read once per layer for the whole batch of P tokens. Decode processes 1 token per sequence per step, so the same weight bytes are re-read per step and arithmetic intensity is ~O(batch).

Design (one factor at a time):
- Independent variable: prompt length P in {128, 512, 2048, 8192} tokens, max_tokens=1 so the step is prefill-dominated.
- Control arm: P=128 fixed, decode length D in {1, 64, 256} to isolate decode cost.
- Fixed: batch=1, tensor-parallel degree, KV dtype, chunked-prefill setting, GPU clocks locked (nvidia-smi -lgc), same server process, warm cache (discard first 3 iterations).
- Repetitions: >=20 timed iterations per cell; report median and p95, not mean.
- Measured: TTFT (ms), prefill throughput (prompt tok/s), achieved TFLOP/s vs A30 BF16 peak (~165 TFLOP/s dense), and DRAM read bandwidth vs ~933 GB/s HBM2 peak, via Nsight Systems / DCGM (DRAM_ACTIVE, SM occupancy).

Predictions (falsifiable):
- H1: prefill time is ~linear in P in the mid range and achieved TFLOP/s utilization rises with P toward a plateau; DRAM utilization stays well below SM utilization. Falsified if TFLOP/s stays flat and DRAM utilization saturates first.
- H2: at large P, attention cost grows super-linearly (O(P^2) term) and TTFT bends upward. Falsified if TTFT stays linear at 8192.
- H3: decode step latency is nearly independent of P (given fixed KV read path is small relative to weights at batch=1). Falsified if decode step time scales with P strongly, which would mean KV-read, not weight-read, dominates.

Boundary conditions: (a) at very small P (<~64 tokens) prefill degenerates to a skinny GEMM and becomes launch/memory-bound, so the compute-bound claim does not hold; (b) chunked prefill or prefix caching invalidates the P-sweep because work is no longer proportional to P; (c) at large P, KV cache allocation may hit the 24 GB limit and trigger preemption, which contaminates timing.

Evidence to collect: nvidia-smi clock/power logs (thermal or power capping on A30 at 165 W invalidates comparisons), server-side per-request TTFT/ITL, Nsight kernel breakdown, KV-cache utilization, and a confirmation that no preemption or recompute events occurred.

Rollback/abort gate: abort and re-run if GPU clocks vary >5% across cells, if p95/median > 1.5 for any cell, or if any preemption is logged; do not report results from a run with concurrent tenants on the GPU.

No falsifiable prediction or rollback gate is given, so the answer is not actionable in an operational context.

Numbers cited in the corrected answer (A30 peak BF16/HBM2 bandwidth, model byte sizes) are vendor-spec or arithmetic estimates, not measurements on this cluster; they must be re-measured before being used as thresholds.

GPU counters: DCGM DRAM_ACTIVE / SM occupancy, clock and power logs to exclude throttling.
KV-cache utilization, prefix-cache hit rate, and preemption/recompute counters.
Exact model, dtype, server version, and config diff for the compared runs.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating prefill. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer:
Runbook: investigating prefill (TTFT) regressions.

Scope assumption: continuous-batching LLM server (vLLM-class) on 8xA30 24GB, PCIe, BF16 weights. All thresholds below are placeholders to be replaced by your measured baseline; do not treat them as platform facts.

Mechanism to keep in mind: prefill is the single parallel forward pass over all prompt tokens. Its cost is dominated by dense GEMMs plus an O(P^2) attention term, and it competes with decode for the same SMs. A TTFT regression is therefore usually one of: (1) longer prompts, (2) lost prefix-cache hits, (3) prefill queueing behind other requests, (4) reduced clocks/power cap, (5) KV-cache pressure causing preemption/recompute.

Triage steps:
1. Confirm the regression is real: compare p50/p95 TTFT over >=200 requests against a stored baseline from the same model and config. A single slow request is not a signal.
2. Segment by prompt length. If TTFT/prompt-token is flat, the change is input distribution, not the server.
3. Check prefix-cache / KV-reuse hit rate. A drop here raises effective P even with unchanged user prompts.
4. Check queueing: waiting time vs execution time in server metrics. If waiting dominates, the fix is scheduling (chunked prefill, prefill/decode disaggregation, admission control), not kernels.
5. Check GPU state: nvidia-smi for clock throttle reasons, power draw vs the ~165 W board limit, ECC errors, and other tenants.
6. Check KV-cache utilization and preemption counters. Preemption converts prefill into repeated recompute.
7. Only then profile kernels (Nsight Systems) and compare achieved TFLOP/s against the previous build.

Boundary condition: when chunked prefill is enabled, TTFT no longer scales linearly with prompt length, and the per-chunk scheduler interleaves decode; comparing TTFT across a config change that toggled chunked prefill is invalid and must be re-baselined.

Evidence required before declaring root cause: baseline vs current TTFT distributions, prompt-length histograms, prefix-cache hit rate, queue-wait breakdown, clock/power logs, preemption counts, and the exact server version/config diff.

Rollback gate: if p95 TTFT exceeds baseline by >20% for 15 continuous minutes at comparable prompt-length distribution and load, roll back the last config/image change first and re-measure before further debugging.

Its cost is dominated by dense GEMMs plus an O(P^2) attention term, and it competes with decode for the same SMs. A TTFT regression is therefore usually one of: (1) longer prompts, (2) lost prefix-cache hits, (3) prefill queueing behind other requests, (4) reduced clocks/power cap, (5) KV-cache pressure causing preemption/recompute.

Triage steps:
1. Confirm the regression is real: compare p50/p95 TTFT over >=200 requests against a stored baseline from the same model and config. A single slow request is not a signal.
2. Segment by prompt length. If TTFT/prompt-token is flat, the change is input distribution, not the server.
3. Check prefix-cache / KV-reuse hit rate. A drop here raises effective P even with unchanged user prompts.
4. Check queueing: waiting time vs execution time in server metrics. If waiting dominates, the fix is scheduling (chunked prefill, prefill/decode disaggregation, admission control), not kernels.
5. Check GPU state: nvidia-smi for clock throttle reasons, power draw vs the ~165 W board limit, ECC errors, and other tenants.
6. Check KV-cache utilization and preemption counters. Preemption converts prefill into repeated recompute.
7. Only then profile kernels (Nsight Systems) and compare achieved TFLOP/s against the previous build.

Boundary condition: when chunked prefill is enabled, TTFT no longer scales linearly with prompt length, and the per-chunk scheduler interleaves decode; comparing TTFT across a config change that toggled chunked prefill is invalid and must be re-baselined.

Evidence required before declaring root cause: baseline vs current TTFT distributions, prompt-length histograms, prefix-cache hit rate, queue-wait breakdown, clock/power logs, preemption counts, and the exact server version/config diff.

Rollback gate: if p95 TTFT exceeds baseline by >20% for 15 continuous minutes at comparable prompt-length distribution and load, roll back the last config/image change first and re-measure before further debugging.

source_user: Define decode and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Definition: decode (the generation or autoregressive phase) is the stage after prefill where the model emits one token per sequence per forward step, appending each new key/value to the KV cache and feeding the sampled token back as input for the next step.

Why it matters: decode determines inter-token latency and dominates total cost for long outputs, and it has fundamentally different hardware behavior from prefill, so a serving stack tuned only for prefill will underperform.

Concrete mechanism: at batch size B, one decode step reads the full model weights (for a 9B BF16 model, ~18 GB) plus the KV cache slice, but performs only B token-rows of GEMM work. Arithmetic intensity is therefore ~O(B) FLOPs per byte of weights, which is far below the machine balance point of an A30 (~165 TFLOP/s BF16 vs ~933 GB/s HBM2, i.e. roughly 170 FLOP/byte). At small B the step time is set by weight-read bandwidth: a lower bound is ~18 GB / 933 GB/s ~= 19 ms per step, nearly independent of B. This is why batching improves decode throughput almost for free until compute or KV capacity binds.

Boundary condition: the memory-bound claim fails once B (or the KV cache read volume at long context) grows enough that attention over the cache, not weight reads, dominates. With very long contexts the per-step KV read scales with B x context_len x layers x 2 x kv_heads x head_dim x dtype_bytes and can exceed weight bytes; then decode becomes KV-bandwidth-bound and larger batches stop being free. On 24 GB A30s, KV capacity usually binds before compute does.

Evidence required to confirm on your system: measured inter-token latency vs batch size, DRAM read bandwidth counters (DCGM DRAM_ACTIVE) during decode, KV-cache utilization, and a check that no preemption or recompute occurred. Falsifiable prediction: step latency should stay roughly flat as B grows from 1 to ~16 at short context; if it rises linearly from B=1, the deployment is not weight-bandwidth-bound and the tuning plan must change.

Operational note: do not change batch size, KV dtype, and context limit at the same time; a single-variable sweep is required to attribute the effect, and any change should be reverted if p95 inter-token latency exceeds the SLO for 10 minutes.
